title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Evolutionary Biology — 2025
origin: curated NEB-pattern set covering every topic of the class-11 evolutionary biology unit

questions.question: Describe the Oparin–Haldane hypothesis of the origin of life and explain the significance of the Miller–Urey experiment.
questions.solution:
Oparin and Haldane proposed that the primitive Earth had a reducing atmosphere of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour with no free oxygen, together with intense ultraviolet radiation, lightning and volcanic heat. These energy sources converted simple gases into organic molecules, which accumulated in the warm ocean as a 'hot dilute soup'; the molecules aggregated into coacervates — membranes enclosing a chemical system — and these became the first primitive cells.
Miller and Urey passed electric sparks through a mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour and obtained amino acids, proving experimentally that the organic building blocks of life can form abiotically under such conditions.

questions.question: Discuss any four lines of evidence of evolution.
questions.solution:
Palaeontological: fossils in rock strata show a sequence of forms and connecting links such as Archaeopteryx, which has both reptilian and avian characters.
Morphological and anatomical: homologous organs — forelimbs of a man, whale, bat and horse built on the same plan — indicate common ancestry, whereas analogous organs (wing of an insect and of a bird) show convergent adaptation.
Embryological: vertebrate embryos share gill slits and a tail at early stages, pointing to common descent.
Biochemical and molecular: the same genetic code, similar proteins such as cytochrome c and similar blood pigments across species show relatedness, and the degree of difference measures how long lineages have been separate.

questions.question: Explain Lamarckism and state why it is rejected.
questions.solution:
Lamarck proposed that organisms have an inborn urge to become more complex, that use of an organ strengthens it while disuse weakens it (use and disuse), and that such acquired characters are inherited by the offspring — the long neck of the giraffe arising from generations of stretching for high leaves.
It is rejected because acquired changes in body cells do not alter the genes of germ cells, so they are not inherited: Weismann cut the tails of mice for many generations and no tailless young appeared, and a blacksmith's strong arms do not produce strong-armed children. The theory also cannot explain why structures useless to the organism exist.

questions.question: State Darwin's theory of natural selection and explain how neo-Darwinism differs from it.
questions.solution:
Darwin's theory rests on overproduction of offspring, variation among them, a struggle for existence, survival of the fittest and inheritance of favourable variations, so that populations gradually change — descent with modification. Later forms of the theory add the modern understanding of heredity.
Neo-Darwinism (the modern synthesis) explains variation as mutation and recombination rather than vague 'variation', identifies genes as the unit of inheritance, and treats evolution as a change in allele frequency in a population under selection, genetic drift, gene flow and mutation, supported by population genetics and the fossil record.

questions.question: Give the position of man in the animal kingdom with the characters that justify it.
questions.solution:
Man (Homo sapiens) is placed in Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Subphylum Vertebrata, Class Mammalia, Order Primates, Family Hominidae, Genus Homo, Species sapiens.
Justification: animal — heterotrophic, no cell wall, moves; chordate — notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord and gill slits at some stage; vertebrate — vertebral column and internal skeleton; mammal — hair, mammary glands, warm blood, diaphragm, three middle-ear bones and a four-chambered heart; primate — grasping hands, opposable thumb, forward-facing eyes with stereoscopic vision, large brain, nails instead of claws and usually one young per birth.

questions.question: Give four differences between old-world monkeys and new-world monkeys.
questions.solution:
1. Nose: narrow, downward-pointing nostrils in old-world monkeys; broad, flat, sideways-facing nostrils in new-world monkeys.
2. Tail: never prehensile in old-world monkeys; often prehensile (gripping) in new-world monkeys.
3. Distribution: Africa and Asia against Central and South America.
4. Teeth and thumb: old-world monkeys have two premolars and opposable thumbs; new-world monkeys have three premolars and thumbs that do not oppose as fully.
Examples: rhesus monkey and baboon (old world); spider monkey and marmoset (new world).

questions.question: Differentiate apes from man, and trace the evolution of modern man from the anthropoid ancestor.
questions.solution:
Apes have a semi-erect posture with longer arms than legs, a prognathous face with a prominent brow ridge, a C-shaped spine, a smaller brain (about 400–500 cm³), no chin and body hair; man is fully erect with longer legs, a flat face, an S-shaped spine, a brain of about 1,350–1,400 cm³, a chin and sparse hair, and possesses speech and culture.
The line runs Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus → Australopithecus africanus (bipedal, small brain) → Homo habilis (stone tools, 650 cm³) → Homo erectus (fire, larger brain, Java and Peking man) → Neanderthal man (burial, cold adaptation) → Cro-Magnon and finally Homo sapiens, with brain size, tool use and culture increasing along the line.

questions.question: Distinguish homologous from analogous organs with one example each, and state what each proves.
questions.solution:
Homologous organs have the same basic structure and embryonic origin but different functions — the forelimbs of man, bat, whale and horse. They show divergent evolution from a common ancestor.
Analogous organs have different structure and origin but similar function — the wing of an insect and the wing of a bird, or the eye of an octopus and of a fish. They show convergent evolution, in which unrelated organisms adapt to a similar way of life; they are evidence of adaptation, not of ancestry.
